description: Space Heritage Explorer is an interactive digital platform that discovers and preserves human-made objects left behind on the Moon and Mars. Using NASA's open data, interactive maps, 3D models, historical timelines, and an AI-powered Space Historian, users can explore abandoned spacecraft, rovers, scientific instruments, and the stories behind humanity's space exploration missions. Our goal is to preserve space heritage and inspire future explorers.
summary: Space Heritage Explorer is an interactive web platform that documents and preserves the human-made objects left on the Moon and Mars, such as landers, rovers, instruments, and impact sites. It has 3D Moon and Mars pages showing where each artifact and mission event sits, a gamified Explorer section where users read mission information and play multi-level quizzes to earn scores, and an AI Space Historian chatbot. The chatbot is a retrieval-augmented (RAG) assistant built on NASA, ISRO, and ESA sources. Every answer carries citations to official agency pages, and a citation checker flags unsupported claims. The project makes scattered space-agency information easy to explore, supports education and public awareness of space heritage, and encourages learners to engage with humanity’s exploration history. It addresses the challenge by turning NASA open data into a trustworthy, interactive learning experience.
details:
What it does

  • Home page and accounts: two roles, normal users and admins. Users have saved chat history, and admins manage sync, knowledge graph, and evaluation tools.
  • Moon and Mars pages: an interactive 3D Moon and Mars showing objects left by astronauts and missions, along with key events.
  • Explorer page: users read mission information, then play quizzes across different levels and gain scores.
  • Space Historian (RAG chatbot): answers questions about missions and artifacts using cited sources.
  • Virtual Moon Journey : an interactive virtual journey across the Moon, [one line on what users see and do]” under What it does.

How the AI works

  • Sources: it indexes NASA, ISRO, and ESA web pages and PDFs, plus the NASA Image Library and APOD.
  • Retrieval: hybrid search combines pgvector semantic search with full-text keyword search on Neon, merged by rank fusion. Metadata filters cover organisation, mission (e.g. Apollo 11, Chandrayaan-3), and date. “X vs Y” questions are split into one retrieval per mission or agency.
  • Trust and citations: it cites only HTTPS pages on nasa.gov, isro.gov.in, and esa.int. It uses [SOURCE n] markers, strips invalid ones, and reports uncited sentences.
  • Multi-agent research: a planner, NASA/ISRO/ESA specialist agents, a reviewer that finds agreements and contradictions, and a synthesizer.
  • Knowledge graph and timeline: it extracts facts and dates with grounding checks against hallucination.
  • Data freshness: old chunks are marked superseded rather than deleted, changes are logged, and a daily cron sync is protected by a database lock so syncs never overlap.
  • Reliability: Gemini calls use retries, model fallback, and cooldowns, with a busy-state reply that still lists sources. Reranking is optional.
  • Quality and security: an evaluation harness measures retrieval hit rate, citation coverage, fact recall, and hallucination rate. Admin-token protection and per-IP rate limits guard sensitive endpoints.

Benefits and impact: It gives students, educators, and the public a free, trustworthy way to learn about off-world human heritage. It combines multi-agency knowledge in one place and shows that AI answers can be verifiable instead of guessed.

Tools and technology: React (front end), FastAPI (back end), PostgreSQL on Neon with pgvector, Google Gemini API, [3D library, e.g. Three.js / react-three-fiber], [hosting platform].

Creativity: It treats the objects left in space as cultural heritage. It combines 3D exploration, gamified learning, and a citation-verified multi-agent AI in one platform, with data from three space agencies.

Factors considered: accuracy and hallucination control, source trust, accessibility for non-experts, rate limiting and security, and system reliability under heavy AI load.
